extracted.intended_audience: general public and people interested in personal injury/tort cases
extracted.subtask_description: A narrative explanation and fact-by-fact rebuttal of common misconceptions about the Stella Liebeck v. McDonald’s hot coffee lawsuit, highlighting legal and factual criteria that made the case legitimate. The page summarizes injuries, corporate policy, settlement efforts, trial evidence, and aftermath.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coffee temperature as a safety hazard
rubrics_metrics.description: At the time of the incident, all McDonald’s restaurants were required to serve coffee between 180 and 190 degrees. At this temperature, spilled coffee causes third-degree burns in less than 3 seconds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare vendor brewing/serving temperatures to industry/home norms to assess danger: most other restaurants served coffee at ~160°F (20 seconds to third-degree burns) and home brewers at 135–150°F. The page uses temperature and time-to-burn science to show the product was unreasonably dangerous at McDonald’s standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Severity and scope of plaintiff's injuries
rubrics_metrics.description: Stella suffered third-degree burns on more than 16% of her body, including inner thighs, genitals, and buttocks, with burns down to muscle and fatty tissue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use medical details as a metric of seriousness: hospitalization (8 days), skin grafts, extensive treatment, and a two-year recovery period demonstrate substantial physical harm supporting damages and countering claims of triviality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior customer complaints as evidence of company knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: At least 700 other people informed McDonald’s that they had been burned by McDonald’s coffee before Stella.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Number and content of prior complaints are used to show the company knew of the risk. A high volume of prior reports supports liability and potential punitive damages because it evidences awareness and failure to act.

rubrics_metrics.name: Company response to settlement and safety requests
rubrics_metrics.description: Stella spent 6 months trying to settle for $20,000 and then $15,000 to cover medical expenses; McDonald’s offered $800 and refused to lower coffee temperature when asked.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Documented settlement negotiations and refusal to change a dangerous policy are evaluative signs: plaintiff attempted reasonable resolution, and the defendant’s low offer/refusal to mitigate can indicate disregard for safety and inform juror sympathy and punitive-award justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gross negligence standard (legal threshold)
rubrics_metrics.description: A person or business acts with gross negligence if they act with a 'reckless disregard for the safety of others.' The lawsuit alleged McDonald’s was 'grossly negligent' for selling coffee that was 'unreasonably dangerous.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the gross negligence definition to facts (high temperature, prior complaints, refusal to change practice) when assessing whether conduct rises above ordinary carelessness to justify punitive relief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trial evidence requirements: corporate policy and documentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence at trial showed McDonald’s required franchisees to keep coffee heated between 180–190 degrees and that the restaurant received more than 700 complaints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proving liability often depends on documentary and testimonial evidence of company policies and complaint histories. The page highlights the importance of adducing company directives and records to prove knowledge and willful conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Damages and remittitur as measures of legal outcome
rubrics_metrics.description: The jury awarded $200,000 in compensatory damages (reduced to $160,000 for 20% plaintiff fault) and $2.7 million in punitive damages (reduced to $480,000 by the judge via remittitur); the case later settled for under $600,000.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compensatory and punitive awards, and judicial remittitur, reflect how juries and judges translate facts into monetary relief. These numbers are used to evaluate the seriousness of the misconduct and to counter simplistic 'million-dollar frivolous suit' narratives by showing how awards were adjusted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparative time-to-burn metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: Most other restaurants serve coffee at 160 degrees, which takes 20 seconds to cause third-degree burns (usually enough time to wipe away the coffee). Home coffee makers typically brew coffee at about 135–150 degrees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use comparative benchmarks to assess whether a vendor’s practice deviates from ordinary industry standards. Longer time-to-burn at lower temperatures supports an argument that McDonald’s higher serving temperature was unreasonable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Context of plaintiff behavior and fault allocation
rubrics_metrics.description: Stella was sitting in the passenger seat of her grandson’s parked car, attempting to remove the lid to add cream while holding the cup between her knees, when the cup tipped and spilled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detailing the circumstances (e.g., car parked, not driving) addresses questions of contributory fault and helps explain why the incident was not simply an avoidable mishap; the jury found 20% plaintiff fault, illustrating how context influences fault allocation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Media framing and public perception versus legal facts
rubrics_metrics.description: After the trial a small article led to widespread, increasingly inaccurate coverage; reputable outlets described the lawsuit as 'the poster child of excessive lawsuits.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that media shorthand can distort legal nuance. When evaluating or explaining a case, present factual context (injury severity, company knowledge, settlement attempts, evidence) to correct or prevent misperception about frivolousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Long-term impact on plaintiff beyond monetary relief
rubrics_metrics.description: Stella died at 91; her daughter said 'the burns and court proceedings took their toll' and that Stella had 'no quality of life' after the trial, though the settlement helped pay for a live-in nurse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider non-economic harms (quality of life, long-term care needs) as part of assessing the real-world consequences of injuries and the adequacy of remedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precedential and subsequent litigation context
rubrics_metrics.description: Since the verdict, numerous lawsuits have been filed against other coffee vendors; most involved lower temperatures and were unsuccessful, though some high-award cases (e.g., a $50 million tea case) have drawn attention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use subsequent case outcomes to understand how facts (temperature, injury severity) affect success. The page implies that many later suits failed because they lacked the extreme facts present in Liebeck’s case.
